agent.name: Emerging Technology Diffusion Agent
agent.specialty: Rogers diffusion, application and peer diffusion, and bounded organizational timing

analytical_question: As of the 2026-11-01 evidence snapshot, how far has LLM-based generative AI diffused generally and in human-reviewed code suggestions, explanations, test drafting and bounded refactoring, and what does that imply for reversible experimentation over a hypothetical six-month horizon at an AI-native software startup? The target social system for peer comparison is comparable AI-native startup engineering teams, geography unspecified. Distinguish individual access, current use, recurring task use, authorized team/firm deployment and industry penetration; organization-level adoption is not established.
general_et_finding: The shared snapshot prepared 2026-11-01 supports substantial self-reported AI use among surveyed technical workers, not a global LLM-only diffusion stage. E1-C1 reports 90% current workplace AI use among surveyed technology professionals (nearly 5,000 worldwide in the survey overall, exact item denominator and country weighting not reported); E1-C2 reports 60% of surveyed AI users using AI about half the time or more when confronting tasks over the prior three months, a conditional individual recurring-use frequency, not daily use or cohort retention. E4-C1 reports 75.9% reliance on AI in at least part of a daily professional responsibility in its 2024 respondent item; E4-C2 reports 74.9% AI reliance for coding tasks among respondents who write code. These measures go beyond availability but cover broad AI, not LLM-only use, and do not verify authorized firm deployment or industry penetration. E2-C1 restates E4 rather than adding an independent 2025 survey. D1/D2 show vendor-described access and integration channels, not population adoption. Across Rogers categories, innovators may try tools before evidence accumulates; early adopters may initiate bounded use; early majority would require peer-relative timing and credible normalization; late majority may adopt after widespread peer legitimacy; laggards would be last within a defined social system. These are conceptual timing categories, not percentages measured by these sources. Without a comparable-population sampling frame, adoption timing and sustained-use definition, none of the five shares, an exact present category, chasm crossing, saturation or S-curve can be assigned for global LLMs, software firms or this startup. The 2024 and 2025 adoption observations warrant refresh under the agent’s 12-month review policy; a 2026 publication about students is not a new professional prevalence observation. No growth rate can be calculated by comparing E4 with E1.
application_finding: Application: human-reviewed coding suggestions, explanation, test drafting and bounded refactoring, not autonomous engineering. E4-C2 is relevant historical individual coding-task reliance, but it measures broad AI support among code-writing respondents, not LLM-only routine use or authorized deployments at comparable AI-native startups. D1/D2 document coding-assistant product channels. There is no dated peer-company numerator/denominator, geographic frame, team penetration, seat-to-active-use conversion, duration or verified workflow outcomes; the application’s exact Rogers stage and peer position remain unresolved. Five diffusion characteristics: (1) Relative advantage — Observation: E4-C2 documents task reliance, not quality-adjusted advantage; E2 reports observational analyses, not causal improvement. Direction: potentially accelerating but uncertain. Mechanism: faster drafting and explanations could reduce effort while review, defects or rework offset gains. Condition: measure comparable tasks’ time, correctness, security defects and rework against a baseline. Confidence: low for net benefit. (2) Compatibility — Observation: D2 issuer describes VS Code inline/chat/agent integration and enterprise-admin access, not local adoption. Direction: potentially accelerating for familiar editor workflows, mixed when policy, repositories and customer confidentiality conflict. Mechanism: familiar interfaces lower switching friction but approved access and data policies determine actual fit. Condition: verify local IDE/repository compatibility, security policy, permissions and customer commitments. Confidence: moderate for described product features, low for local fit. (3) Complexity — Observation: D2 lists extension/version and model-access dependencies; E3-C1 describes student verification and skill-preservation practices. Direction: mixed/inhibiting without support. Mechanism: prompting, evaluating outputs, dependencies, code review, training and integration create work beyond easy sign-up. Condition: record setup burden, verification time, staff capacity and version stability. Confidence: moderate for documented dependencies, low for their effects at this startup. (4) Trialability — Observation: D2 issuer describes free sign-up and access channels, while D1 shows historical general availability. Direction: potentially accelerating if a bounded, reversible, permissioned pilot is possible; access alone is not adoption. Mechanism: isolation and rollback allow learning without enterprise-wide commitment. Condition: approve data boundaries, licensing/entitlements, pilot owners and rollback. Confidence: moderate for described access, low for realized ease/cost. (5) Observability — Observation: no supplied controlled local evaluation or trustworthy comparable-startup outcomes; E2-C3 recommends telemetry beyond licenses/DAU but does not supply it. Direction: unknown/mixed. Mechanism: visible demos and apparent code speed may aid communication but conceal defect and rework costs; credible peer results and audited local quality metrics would strengthen learning. Condition: capture accepted suggestions, recurring meaningful use, quality-adjusted outcomes and explainable peer comparisons. Confidence: low. Diffusion mechanisms: D1/D2 support the existence of vendor/editor channels and dependencies, possible accelerators through distribution and complementary developer tooling but not measured uptake effects; neither a repository nor API implies universal standards. Hypothesized, not observed here: a respected senior engineer as opinion leader, a technical founder as change agent, code-review discussions and engineering communities as channels, and comparable-startup demonstrations as peer influence. Validate influence by engineers’ observed decisions rather than labels. Potential inhibitors include staff-limited governance, review burden, confidentiality/IP risk, vendor lock-in and concerns about skill erosion (the last supported as a student-study theme, not a measured startup prevalence). D3 concerns a medical model, not coding penetration or clinical documentation adoption.
organization_specific_finding: The startup is a hypothetical AI-native organization with an expressly aggressive Early Adopter posture. Technical familiarity, adaptable workflows, constrained staff/governance and ability to isolate experiments are scenario assumptions, not findings of existing use. Under Rogers, its willingness to learn early is behavior consistent with a possible early-adopter role; AI-native identity and the posture label cannot establish observed adoption date, peer-relative category or current use. Comparable peers are AI-native startup engineering teams in the same coding workflow and geography, currently unspecified; no credible peer deployment denominator or local rank is available. Its flexible workflows and risk tolerance could make a narrowly scoped, reversible pilot defensible earlier than a fast follower would standardize, but limited review capacity and customer-facing code/security/IP consequences may make broad reliance premature. Within a hypothetical six months, the earliest stage is permissioned task-level learning with engineer review, followed only conditionally by broader team evaluation when repeat-use and quality gates are passed. The startup’s posture alters acceptable experimentation timing, not the E1–E4 general adoption statistics or the technology’s population Rogers stage.

evidence.claim: E1-C1: 90% of surveyed technology professionals reported current AI use at work; not 90% of firms or LLM-only users.
evidence.date_or_recency: 2025 publication and survey context; exact fieldwork dates unreported; older than 12-month review flag as of 2026-11-01
evidence.evidence_type: Original issuer cross-sectional self-report survey infographic and inspected questionnaire
evidence.notes: DORA/Google Cloud; nearly 5,000 technology professionals worldwide overall; exact item n, geography weighting, sampling/recruitment and 2025 full methods not reported in supplied evidence. Broader AI tools and individual current use only. Vendor-affiliated, not an organization census.

evidence.claim: E1-C2: 60% of surveyed AI users reported using AI about half the time or more when encountering a task/problem over the prior three months.
evidence.date_or_recency: 2025 publication and survey context; retrospective three-month recall; exact fieldwork dates unreported
evidence.notes: Denominator is surveyed AI users, not all surveyed professionals, firms or daily active users; item n unknown. Recall frequency is not observed telemetry, three-month cohort persistence or authorized firm rollout. DORA/Google Cloud affiliation and unknown 2025 recruitment/weighting limit generalization.

evidence.claim: E4-C1: 75.9% of 2024 DORA respondents reported at least partial AI reliance in one or more daily professional responsibilities.
evidence.date_or_recency: 2024 annual survey; exact fieldwork dates and publication day unreported; historical as of November 2026
evidence.evidence_type: Original inspected report and self-report survey
evidence.notes: Nearly 3,000 working professionals across 104 countries overall; exact item n not reported. Organic blogs/email/social/snowball plus supplemental panels; three survey flows, so overall n is not item n. Broad AI task reliance, not a daily-active metric, LLM-only use or company deployment.

evidence.claim: E4-C2: 74.9% of respondents whose responsibilities include writing code reported some AI reliance for that task.
evidence.date_or_recency: 2024 annual survey; exact fieldwork dates unreported; refresh needed
evidence.evidence_type: Original inspected report, coding-task conditional survey item
evidence.notes: Denominator restricted to respondents who write code; exact item n not given. Self-selected international technology-oriented sample and broad AI wording limit peer representativeness and current LLM-only inference. Not an organization-level sustained-use result.

evidence.claim: E4-C3: Survey-method context includes organic and supplemental-panel recruitment, three survey flows, nearly 3,000 participants from 104 countries.
evidence.date_or_recency: 2024 report v.2024.3; precise publication day unverified
evidence.notes: Printed pages 91, 97 and 102; recruitment and survey-flow design constrain generalization. Randomized survey flows are not randomized AI interventions.

evidence.claim: E2-C1/C2: Repeats rounded 76% 2024 AI reliance and describes team incorporation as respondent-estimated share of team work supported by AI in last three months.
evidence.date_or_recency: Released March 2025; underlying 2024 survey and September 2024 interviews
evidence.evidence_type: Issuer observational analysis and respondent-estimated team-work measure
evidence.notes: Same underlying E4 reliance, not independent 2025 replication. Underlying 2024 survey nearly 3,000 professionals in 104 countries; supplemental interviews with 10 development professionals. Team-work share is not share of companies deployed. No randomized intervention or causal productivity magnitude established.

evidence.claim: E2-C3: Recommends license and DAU tracking while warning those alone do not establish coding-assistant impact.
evidence.date_or_recency: March 2025 release, using 2024 evidence; PDF v.2025.2
evidence.evidence_type: Original publisher measurement guidance, not collected adoption data
evidence.notes: Printed page 41. No denominator or observed local telemetry; DORA/Google Cloud issuer and observational scope. Proposed instrumentation must not be counted as an empirical result.

evidence.claim: E3-C1: Selected Berkeley students describe moderated AI use, unassisted problem-solving, verification and skill/dependence concerns.
evidence.date_or_recency: Published/updated 2026-02-17; eight-month project, exact fieldwork dates unreported
evidence.evidence_type: Original issuer-described student mixed-methods qualitative study
evidence.notes: UC Berkeley EECS/Design/Data Science participants; n, sampling frame and response rate not reported. Supports hypotheses about training and trust, not professional prevalence, organization adoption or causal effects; same DORA author ecosystem.

evidence.claim: D1: Historical GitHub Copilot preview README states general availability and links to a dated announcement.
evidence.date_or_recency: Undated archived README; retrieved 2026-11-02T00:51:23.545126+00:00; linked 2022-06-21 announcement not inspected
evidence.notes: Historical product access and vendor channel only; no sampling frame, user denominator, adoption or retention measure. Shares GitHub/Microsoft corporate ecosystem with D2; access-to-trial effect is inference.

evidence.claim: D2: Archived VS Code Copilot Chat README describes inline, chat and agent workflows, free signup, enterprise access and update/version dependencies.
evidence.notes: Describes potential compatibility, trial access and complexity, not verified current pricing/functionality, effectiveness or use prevalence. Archived and vendor-authored; same ecosystem as D1. Effect on startup diffusion remains inference.

evidence.claim: D3: MedGemma README describes medical text/image variants, notebooks and links, not clinical documentation deployment.
evidence.evidence_type: Issuer technical/model repository description; negative scope boundary
evidence.notes: Google Health source; no hospital or clinician adoption denominator, observed use, independently verified clinical benefit or ambient-scribe evidence. Model ecosystem cannot establish the weak hospital diffusion claim.

contrary_evidence_or_limitations: The 2025 E1 and 2024 E4 observed adoption measures concern broad AI and sampled individuals, with nonrepresentative or unknown recruitment features; they do not support current LLM-only penetration or a Rogers stage for comparable startup firms.
E1’s 60% has surveyed AI users as its denominator and retrospective frequency is neither daily-active telemetry nor sustained cohort retention; E4’s 74.9% is confined to code-writing respondents.

E2’s 76% summarizes E4’s 75.9% rather than independently confirming it; observational associations and respondent-perceived team incorporation do not prove causal productivity, actual organizational rollout or a cross-year growth rate.
E3 records student concerns about verification and skill dependence, providing a counterweight to speed enthusiasm but no measured frequency or effect among startup engineers.

D1/D2 are historical/archived vendor descriptions and D3 concerns medical model access; none verifies current entitlement, startup outcomes, peer firm deployment, hospital ambient documentation prevalence or a universal interoperability standard.

The hypothetical startup has no provided baseline, actual usage records, geographic comparator frame, peer denominator, security approval or accountable decision owner; absence of data is not evidence of nonuse.
confidence_and_uncertainty: Moderate confidence that the original DORA issuer materials report substantial broad-AI individual use among surveyed technical workers, but low confidence that those samples represent current 2026 LLM-only population prevalence or an exact Rogers stage. The 2024/2025 adoption observations exceed a 12-month review window by November 2026; E1 2025 full recruitment/methods, item n, exact fieldwork dates and weighting are not reported in supplied evidence. Moderate confidence in the existence of issuer-described coding assistant access/integration channels, low confidence in their causal diffusion effect, coding quality advantage or sustained comparable-startup peer penetration. Low confidence in startup-specific timing outcomes because organization facts beyond identity/posture are scenario assumptions and no local measurement exists. The qualitative pilot timing judgment is conditional, not an empirical forecast.
value_opportunity_implication: A small, reversible trial could reveal whether code explanation, test drafting, suggestions and bounded refactoring improve quality-adjusted development throughput and learning for this hypothetical startup. Treat apparent speed, enthusiasm and individual usage as candidate signals only. Compare task completion and review/rework burden, defect/security findings and developer skill retention with an agreed local baseline; do not invent an ROI, productivity uplift or adoption-to-benefit causal estimate.
risk_governance_implication: Require named human reviewers before merging generated code, authorized repository/data boundaries, confidentiality/IP checks, dependency/security review, incident and rollback paths, and explicit customer-impact evaluation. Limited startup staff and flexibility can increase both experimentation capacity and governance gaps. Legal, security and policy acceptability must be decided by responsible owners; neither the existence of vendor admin controls nor this specialist assessment is certification or authorization.
recommendation_management_implication: Conditional diffusion-timing advice only: appoint a technical evaluation owner and an accountable security/data reviewer; inventory the startup’s actual use, eligible engineers, permissioned tools, workflows and baseline. Start with isolated, low-consequence code suggestions, explanations and test drafts for a proposed short learning cycle within the six-month horizon; require human review and preserved rollback. Before wider team reliance, require repeated meaningful-use/retention observations, quality-adjusted comparison against baseline, approved handling of code/data, review capacity and credible comparable-peer evidence. Delay, narrow or reverse expansion if defects, rework, confidentiality concerns, unsupported model/version changes or reviewer overload appear. Agree a reassessment event/date at pilot setup (for example, after two review cycles), not a claimed evidence-backed deadline. This is not a full adoption decision; the Adoption Agent and accountable management retain that authority.
change_monitoring_triggers: Technical evaluation owner: establish baseline and weekly eligible, enabled, trialing and meaningful active users by engineering team; separate seat allocation from actual use and track repeat cohorts over multiple weeks.

Engineering lead and code reviewers: record comparable-task completion time, generated-code acceptance, tests, defect/security severity, rework and reviewer effort; review after each proposed pilot cycle and before scope expansion.

Security/data owner: monitor repository permissions, confidential-data exposures, license terms, vendor/update changes and documented approval or incidents; pause affected workflow on unacceptable events.

Research/evaluation owner: request a dated original survey or administrative study of comparable AI-native software firms with geography, firm denominator, authorized routine-use definition, sampling and observation period; refresh 2024/2025 measures rather than treating archived data as current.

Technical founder and governance owner: at pilot kickoff schedule a proposed reassessment after two bounded review cycles and no later than the six-month planning review; set any numerical pass/fail thresholds locally before inspecting results.
abstention_or_more_information_needed: Abstain from numerical LLM-only penetration, exact global or peer Rogers category, chasm crossing, S-curve location and saturation. Request current dated original population surveys with LLM-specific current/recurring-use questions, geographic/sector boundaries, recruitment, item denominators, fieldwork dates and timing distributions.

Abstain from claiming most comparable AI-native software firms routinely deploy LLM coding assistants, or from ranking this startup against peers. Request a defined sample of comparable firms, geographic frame, institution-level authorized-deployment denominator, coding workflow scope, repeated use/retention evidence and peer adoption dates.

Abstain from claiming most comparable hospitals now routinely use LLM-assisted clinical documentation. E1/E4 concern technology workers and D3 a medical-model ecosystem, not this workflow. Request a dated original hospital-level survey or administrative dataset specifying geographic frame, sampled hospitals/specialties, clinician/documentation-use definition, institutional denominator and longitudinal routine-use evidence.

Abstain from estimating causal productivity magnitude, ROI or an exact forecast adoption date for this startup. Request an approved local comparison of matched tasks with quality, security and rework measurements, and a responsible owner for interpretation.

Request the startup’s actual baseline adoption, engineering headcount/eligibility, current license/access, data policy, approved repositories, geography, accountable evaluation and security decision owners, pilot scope and agreed reassessment date. Missing information narrows the timing claim; it does not establish nonuse.
